python-fundamentals.definition: A Python program is a set of instructions the interpreter executes in order.
python-fundamentals.why: Learning to predict what a line will print gives you a fast way to test an idea and spot mistakes before building a larger program.
python-fundamentals.explanation: An expression produces a value. When Python reaches print(), it evaluates the expressions inside the parentheses and writes their values to the output. Text inside quotes is a literal. A line beginning with # is a comment for the reader.
python-fundamentals.usage: Use a two-line journal entry to tell a reader what you studied and how much time you spent.

examples.title: Write a journal entry
examples.code:
print("Hello, learner!")
print("Today I studied Python.")
examples.output:
Hello, learner!
Today I studied Python.

mistakes: Python treats Print and print as different names.
edges: An empty print() writes a blank line.
useCases: Learning journal
Use a two-line journal entry to tell a reader what you studied and how much time you spent.
practices: Run one small change at a time and predict the output first.
python-fundamentals.interview: How does printing 2 + 3 differ from printing "2 + 3"? The first evaluates arithmetic. The second displays the literal characters.
python-fundamentals.miniProject: Print your study topic and the total of two study sessions.
exercises: Print your study topic and the total of two study sessions.
Print the same sentence on two different lines using two calls.

variables.definition: A variable is a name bound to a value. Values have types such as int, float, str and bool.
variables.why: A name lets you reuse a value, change it in one place and describe its role to the next reader.
variables.explanation: Python evaluates the right side of = before binding the name on the left. A later assignment rebinds the name. Quotes make "42" text, even though it looks numeric. Convert at the boundary where text enters a calculation.
variables.usage: A profile stores a name as text, years of experience as a number and active status as a Boolean.

examples.title: Create a profile
examples.code:
name = "Mira"
years = 2
active = True
print(name, years, active)

mistakes: Using = to compare values changes the meaning of the statement. Use == to test equality.
edges: int("2.5") raises ValueError because the text represents a decimal.
useCases: Employee profile
A profile stores a name as text, years of experience as a number and active status as a Boolean.
practices: Give variables descriptive names such as study_minutes and keep their units visible.
variables.interview: What happens to hours after int(hours)? The conversion returns a new integer. The original binding still refers to the string.
variables.miniProject: Create an employee profile and print an introduction using its fields.
exercises: Create an employee profile and print an introduction using its fields.
Convert a study-time field from text to minutes and add a 15-minute practice session.

strings.definition: A string is an immutable sequence of Unicode code points. Use str to represent names, messages, filenames and other text.
strings.why: Forms, filenames, chat messages and model prompts all arrive as text. Understanding where characters start and stop prevents subtle bugs when cleaning or extracting information.
strings.explanation: Single and double quotes create equivalent strings. Choose the quote that keeps the text readable. Triple quotes preserve newlines. Positions start at zero and negative indices count back from the end. A slice selects a range and excludes its stop. Methods return values you can save or pass to another operation. Concatenation with + combines strings. An f-string inserts expressions between braces. split() with no argument treats runs of whitespace as one separator. join() places its separator between each item. Python's < and > compare strings lexicographically by code point, so a machine comparison can differ from human alphabetical ordering.
strings.syntax:
text = "AI Career Lab"
text[start:stop:step]  # start, stop and step are integer positions
message = f"Welcome to {text}!"
strings.usage: A formatter can clean up a name, collapse whitespace and create a consistent display message without altering the original input.

examples.title: Choose quotes and preserve newlines
examples.code:
single = 'Python'
double = "It's ready"
multiline = """line one
line two"""
print(single, double)
print(multiline)
examples.output:
Python It's ready
line one
line two

examples.title: Escape quotes, tabs and line breaks
Compare normalized Unicode
examples.code:
import unicodedata
composed = "é"
decomposed = "e\u0301"
print(len(composed), len(decomposed))
print(composed == decomposed)
print(unicodedata.normalize("NFC", decomposed) == composed)

examples.title: Trace a palindrome check
examples.code:
text = "Level"
key = text.casefold()
print(key, key[::-1])
print(key == key[::-1])

examples.title: Count repeated characters

mistakes: Assigning word[0] = "p" raises TypeError. Build a new string from pieces.
strip('ab') removes those characters repeatedly from either end. Use removeprefix('ab') when you mean one literal prefix.
Concatenating a number with + raises TypeError. Format the number with an f-string or use str().
find() returns -1 on a miss. Test the result before using it as an index.
edges: Indexing an empty string raises IndexError. Slicing it safely produces an empty string.
A slice step of zero raises ValueError. Large nonzero slice bounds are clipped to the string's length.
len() counts Unicode code points. A visible character may span several code points, and reversing a slice can split their display sequence.
''.split() gives an empty list, while ''.split(',') gives a list containing one empty string.
useCases: Normalize search terms while keeping an original display label.
Create consistent filenames, report headings and greeting messages.
Parse delimited text when separators cannot appear in values. Use the csv module for quoted CSV data.
practices: Keep the original input and store cleaned text in a new variable.
Choose a normalization rule that fits the task. Preserve a person's original spelling for display.
Collect many fragments in a list and join them once when assembling larger reports.
strings.interview: What does text[1:4] include? Positions 1, 2 and 3. Which changes if text.replace() is called without saving the result? The original string keeps its value. For a first-unique-character problem, explain a two-pass solution. Count each character once and scan the original order for the first count of one. The runtime is linear in the number of code points. The table uses space proportional to the number of distinct characters.
strings.miniProject: Build a profile text formatter that accepts a name and a role. Strip surrounding whitespace, collapse repeated spaces, preserve the original input and print a greeting using an f-string. Show a clear response for a name containing only spaces.
exercises: Reverse a string while preserving spaces and capitalization.
Decide if a phrase is a palindrome after case folding and removing non-alphanumeric characters.
Count the occurrences of each character, including spaces.
Find the first non-repeating character in original order. Define the result when there is none.

numbers.definition: Python supplies integers for whole numbers and floats for approximate decimal values.
numbers.why: Every calculation depends on the operator and units you choose. Splitting a duration into complete blocks and leftover minutes uses two different operators.
numbers.explanation: Use +, -, * and / for basic arithmetic. Floor division // rounds a quotient down and % gives the remainder. Multiplication runs before addition unless parentheses change the order.
numbers.usage: Convert a number of minutes to hours and minutes using quotient and remainder.
mistakes: The ^ operator performs bitwise XOR. Use ** for exponentiation.
edges: Division by zero raises ZeroDivisionError. Floor division rounds negative results toward negative infinity.
useCases: Study time calculator
Convert a number of minutes to hours and minutes using quotient and remainder.
practices: Use integer counts for quantities with fixed units, such as cents or seconds.
numbers.interview: Why does 7 / 2 produce 3.5 while 7 // 2 produces 3? The operators implement different definitions of division.
numbers.miniProject: Turn a weekly minute total into hours and leftover minutes.
exercises: Turn a weekly minute total into hours and leftover minutes.
Calculate the number of complete five-minute practice blocks in 47 minutes.

predicates.definition: A predicate asks a yes-or-no question about something. “Does this book have a copy available?” is a predicate you can use to decide which books to show.
predicates.why: A precise rule gives the same decision to two people with the same facts. The library can explain a declined hold and point to the exact fact that would change the answer.
prerequisites: No programming experience is needed to follow the library example.
predicates.explanation: Think of a question with a blank in it. “Does ___ have at least one copy?” becomes answerable when you name a book and look up its shelf count. That count is the input. The answer is the result. A computer can ask the question once for every book, just as a librarian can walk down a shelf. The rule stays the same while the answers change with the facts.
predicates.usage: Read copies > 0 from left to right as “is the number of copies greater than zero?” The name available remembers the answer. A later instruction can use that answer to display a button.

examples.title: One copy left at the library
Combine a card check with a stock check
examples.code:
card_valid = False
copies = 3
print(card_valid and copies > 0)

examples.title: Keep only parcels that fit the locker
Give a rule a reusable name
examples.code:
def can_reserve(card_valid, copies):
    return card_valid and copies > 0

print(can_reserve(True, 1))
print(can_reserve(False, 1))

mistakes: Writing > 1 rejects the last copy. Test the values on either side of the boundary.
A comparison such as copies == 1 asks a question. An assignment such as copies = 1 changes which value the name holds.
The text 'False' is a nonempty string. Convert incoming text deliberately before using it as a yes-or-no answer.
edges: Decide how to handle a missing measurement before comparing it with a number.
Python can use a predicate in an if statement. SQL also uses predicates in WHERE, where comparisons with a missing value can be unknown. WHERE keeps rows whose condition is true.
useCases: Find items in stock, grant a discount, verify that a parcel fits, or select rows before a machine-learning calculation.
methods: and requires both answers to be true. or requires at least one. not reverses a yes-or-no answer.
practices: Say the rule aloud first. Write one example it accepts and one it refuses.
Give the rule a question-like name such as can_reserve. Keep checking separate from making the reservation.
predicates.interview: If someone says “up to 5 kg,” ask whether exactly 5 qualifies. Then show what happens at 4, 5 and 6. An example on either side makes the business rule visible.
predicates.miniProject: Build a library hold checker and use it to show the books a member can reserve.
exercises: Check hold eligibility for a valid or expired card and a given stock count.

conditions.definition: A conditional chooses a block of code according to a truth value.
conditions.why: A program becomes responsive to different inputs when it can choose which instructions to execute.
conditions.explanation: An if is tested first. Python evaluates elif clauses in order until one succeeds. The optional else handles every remaining case. Indentation identifies the statements in each branch.
conditions.usage: Choose a revision activity that fits the number of minutes remaining.

examples.title: Choose an activity
Check two conditions
examples.code:
minutes = 15
quiet = True
print(minutes >= 10 and quiet)

mistakes: A broad first condition can make a later, more specific branch unreachable.
edges: Check exact boundary values, such as 10 and 30 in the activity planner.
useCases: Study session planner
Choose a revision activity that fits the number of minutes remaining.
practices: Write down the intended result for each boundary before choosing comparison operators.
conditions.interview: Does a second independent if behave like elif? Two independent conditions may both execute. An if/elif chain chooses at most one branch.
conditions.miniProject: Select one activity for each of three available-time ranges.
exercises: Select one activity for each of three available-time ranges.
Add an option for a zero-minute session and verify each boundary.

loops.definition: A loop repeats a block of code for items in a sequence or while a condition holds.
loops.why: Repeating a calculation with a loop works for both a few records and a long list whose size is unknown when you write the program.
loops.explanation: A for loop binds its loop variable to each item in turn. Initialize a running total before the loop and update it inside. A while loop rechecks its condition before every pass.
loops.usage: Sum the minutes from several study sessions and count how many reached a goal.

examples.title: Accumulate minutes
examples.code:
total = 0
for minutes in [15, 20, 10]:
    total += minutes
print(total)

mistakes: Resetting the accumulator inside the loop erases earlier results.
edges: An empty sequence runs a for loop zero times.
useCases: Session summary
Sum the minutes from several study sessions and count how many reached a goal.
practices: Iterate directly over items when their positions are irrelevant.
loops.interview: Why does range(3) end at 2? The stop is exclusive, giving three values beginning at zero.
loops.miniProject: Count sessions lasting at least 20 minutes and report their total length.
exercises: Count sessions lasting at least 20 minutes and report their total length.
Print a countdown followed by a completion message.

lists.definition: A list is an ordered, mutable collection. Its items can be read, replaced, added and removed.
lists.why: Programs often need to remember a changing collection where order and duplicates both matter.
lists.explanation: Square brackets hold items separated by commas. An index identifies one position. append changes the existing list. Assignment to a second name can point both names at the same list.
lists.usage: Maintain a shopping list as items are added or purchased.

examples.title: Copy before editing
examples.code:
items = ["tea"]
later = items.copy()
later.append("milk")
print(items, later)

mistakes: Assigning items = items.append("tea") replaces the list binding with None.
edges: Accessing position 0 in an empty list raises IndexError.
useCases: Shopping list
Maintain a shopping list as items are added or purchased.
practices: Build a new list when filtering items instead of removing elements while iterating.
lists.interview: How do aliasing and a shallow copy differ? An alias reaches the same list. A shallow copy has a separate outer container but may share nested objects.
lists.miniProject: Build a shopping list and print a numbered summary.
exercises: Build a shopping list and print a numbered summary.
Remove all purchased items while preserving the order of the rest.

tuples.definition: A tuple groups values in a fixed order and prevents replacement of its elements.
tuples.why: A fixed-size group allows related values to travel together and makes unpacking a function's result straightforward.
tuples.explanation: The comma creates a tuple. Unpacking binds names to its positions. A tuple works well for a small fixed record whose positions have a clear meaning.
tuples.usage: Keep a pair of grid coordinates together while passing it to a display function.

examples.title: Unpack a point
examples.code:

x, y = point
print(x + y)

mistakes: Parentheses around a single value do not create a tuple without a comma.
edges: A tuple can contain a list whose contents may still change.
useCases: Coordinate card
Keep a pair of grid coordinates together while passing it to a display function.
practices: Use descriptive unpacked names and use named fields for long records.
tuples.interview: Can a tuple always serve as a dictionary key? Every contained value must also be hashable.
tuples.miniProject: Store three named locations with coordinate pairs.
exercises: Store three named locations with coordinate pairs.

sets.definition: A set is a collection of unique hashable values with fast membership tests.
sets.why: Membership and overlap become direct operations when each distinct value is represented once.
sets.explanation: Repeated values collapse into one set member. Intersection finds shared items. Difference identifies items present in one collection and absent from another.
sets.usage: Find the skills that a learner already has and those still needed for a project.

examples.title: Find overlap

edges: Iteration order is unspecified. Sort when a reproducible display order matters.

practices: Use set operations to express comparisons directly.

dictionaries.definition: A dictionary maps unique hashable keys to associated values.
dictionaries.why: Looking up a record by its identifier stays simple even when the collection grows or its display order changes.
dictionaries.explanation: A lookup retrieves a value using its key. Assigning an existing key replaces its value. get lets you supply a fallback for a missing key.

dictionaries.miniProject: Add, edit and search contacts by name.
exercises: Add, edit and search contacts by name.

functions.definition: A function is a named block of behavior that accepts arguments and can return a result.
functions.why: A calculation that receives inputs and returns a result can serve the interface, an exercise grader and an automated test without being rewritten.
functions.explanation: def introduces the function and its parameter names. A call supplies the actual arguments. return sends a value back to the caller and ends that call. Local variable names belong to the call.
functions.usage: Separate calculations from printing so the same logic can be reused and tested.

exercises: Implement add, subtract and multiply functions for a calculator.

recursion.definition: Recursion solves a problem by calling the same function on a smaller version of it.
recursion.why: Trees and nested collections naturally contain smaller versions of the same structure. Recursion can express that structure directly.
recursion.explanation: Identify the smallest input you can answer immediately. For all other inputs, shrink the remaining problem. Each call waits for the next result before combining it with its own work.
recursion.usage: Count leaves in nested containers where the depth is unknown in advance.

comprehensions.definition: A comprehension builds a new collection using an expression, a loop and an optional filter.
comprehensions.why: A transformation and an optional condition can often be read together more easily than a loop that appends one element at a time.
comprehensions.explanation: Read the for part first to identify each input. Read the if part next to decide whether to keep it. The leading expression computes each resulting item.
comprehensions.syntax: squares = [n*n for n in range(5) if n % 2 == 0]

file-handling.definition: File handling reads or writes streams of text or bytes through a file object.
file-handling.why: A variable disappears after a program exits. Writing a file lets later runs or other tools use the same records.
file-handling.explanation: Use with to guarantee cleanup. Mode w creates or truncates a file, a appends and r reads. Specify the text encoding so readers can decode the same bytes.
file-handling.syntax:
with open("notes.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as file:
    file.write("Study log")
file-handling.usage: Store expense records as one line per entry and read them back in a later step.

exceptions.why: Invalid user input and missing data are ordinary situations that a program can handle without losing unrelated work.
exceptions.explanation: Put the conversion that may fail in try. Handle the expected exception type in except. A finally block runs as the protected block exits and is useful for cleanup.

oop.definition: A class defines a type whose instances can hold state and expose behavior through methods.
oop.why: State and the rules for changing it can live together so every caller uses the same operations to check out or return a book.

modules.definition: A module groups Python definitions under a common name. A package organizes related modules.
modules.why: A shared module gives multiple scripts one maintained implementation of a useful operation.
modules.explanation: import binds the module name so attributes can be accessed through it. from imports a selected name into the current namespace. Python ships with modules for numbers, text, dates and many other tasks.
modules.syntax:

from collections import Counter

virtual-environments.definition: A virtual environment gives a project its own Python interpreter context and package installation directory.
virtual-environments.why: Separating dependencies makes one project easier to reproduce without breaking another project that needs a different package version.
virtual-environments.explanation: Create one using python -m venv .venv. Run that environment's interpreter to install and execute project code. Activation changes which interpreter a shell finds first.
virtual-environments.syntax:

python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip --version
virtual-environments.usage: Keep the packages required by one local application separate from another project's dependencies.
mistakes: Installing with a bare pip can use a different interpreter than the one running the program.
edges: Moving a virtual environment to another path can invalidate embedded paths. Recreate it from its requirements.
useCases: Project environment card
Keep the packages required by one local application separate from another project's dependencies.
practices: Use the intended interpreter with -m pip and keep an explicit dependency file.
virtual-environments.interview: Does activation change your code? It adjusts the shell environment so commands resolve to the project interpreter.

exercises: Record the exact commands for creating and using a Windows project environment.

git.definition: Git records a project's history as snapshots. A GitHub repository can host a shared copy.
git.why: A sequence of meaningful commits lets you inspect, compare and recover previous working versions of a project.
git.explanation: The working tree contains current files. The index holds changes selected for the next commit. A commit saves that selection with a message and parent history.
git.syntax:

git status
git add journal.md
git commit -m "Add study journal"

dsa.definition: A data structure organizes values for access and updates. An algorithm describes how to solve a problem using them.
dsa.why: The same records support different behaviors depending on how they are stored. A queue naturally preserves arrival order while a stack supports undo.
dsa.explanation: A stack removes the most recently added item. A queue removes the earliest. Match the access order to the behavior your application needs.
dsa.syntax:
from collections import deque
pending = deque(["read", "code"])
next_task = pending.popleft()

useCases: Task queue
Process study tasks in arrival order and use a stack to undo recent edits.
practices: Describe the order guarantee your problem requires before picking a container.
dsa.interview: When would a stack be appropriate? It supports last-in-first-out behavior such as undo or depth-first traversal.

complexity.definition: Complexity describes how work and extra storage grow as input size grows.
complexity.why: A solution that works on ten records can become too slow or memory-hungry at ten thousand. Growth rates help you anticipate that change.
complexity.explanation: Count operations in terms of n. A scan grows linearly. Doubling both dimensions of a full pairwise comparison roughly quadruples the comparisons. Ignore constant factors when describing asymptotic growth.
complexity.syntax:
# One visit per item gives O(n) time.
total = 0

routing.explanation: Path parameters identify resources. Query parameters often filter or paginate a collection. A literal path and a parameterized path may both match the same string.
routing.syntax:
from urllib.parse import urlsplit, parse_qs
u = urlsplit("/employees?team=AI")
print(u.path, parse_qs(u.query)["team"][0])
routing.usage: Keep collection filtering separate from fetching a single employee.

examples.title: Read query parameters
examples.code:
from urllib.parse import urlsplit, parse_qs
u = urlsplit("/employees?team=AI")
print(u.path, parse_qs(u.query)["team"][0])

examples.title: Build an encoded query
examples.code:

print(urlencode({"team":"AI Lab"}))

mistakes: Defining a broad dynamic path before a more specific static path can hide the static route.
edges: A valid path used with an unsupported method should be distinguished from an unknown path.
useCases: Employee route map
Keep collection filtering separate from fetching a single employee.
practices: Keep identifiers in paths and optional filters in query parameters.
routing.interview: What distinguishes /employees/7 from /employees?team=AI? The first identifies a resource. The second selects members of a collection.
routing.miniProject: Map list, search and detail operations for an employee directory.
exercises: Map list, search and detail operations for an employee directory.
Verify a static /employees/me route alongside a numeric ID route.

authentication.definition: Authentication establishes identity. Authorization decides whether that identity may perform an action on a resource.
authentication.why: Allow employees to read their own private profile and administrators to manage permitted records.
authentication.explanation: Validate credentials using a trusted mechanism. Then check permissions and ownership on the server for the specific operation.
authentication.usage: Allow employees to read their own private profile and administrators to manage permitted records.

examples.title: Check resource ownership

mistakes: Trusting a role sent by the client lets callers grant themselves privileges.
edges: A valid identity can still lack permission for one particular record.
useCases: Employee access policy
Allow employees to read their own private profile and administrators to manage permitted records.
practices: Deny access by default and evaluate permissions for every protected operation.
authentication.interview: Why verify ownership after login? A valid identity alone does not authorize access to another person's data.
authentication.miniProject: Write an access matrix for owners, colleagues and administrators.
exercises: Write an access matrix for owners, colleagues and administrators.
Exercise each role against the same private employee record.

database-integration.definition: Database integration connects request handling to durable queries and transactions.
database-integration.why: Persist employee edits while preventing request values from altering SQL syntax.
database-integration.explanation: Create a database session for one unit of work. Bind values as parameters, commit related changes together and release resources when the request finishes.
database-integration.syntax:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
print(db.execute("SELECT ? AS name", ("O'Neil",)).fetchone()[0])
database-integration.usage: Persist employee edits while preventing request values from altering SQL syntax.

examples.title: Bind a value
examples.code:

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")

mistakes: Building SQL by interpolating input can turn data into executable query text.
edges: An interrupted request after a commit may leave the client unsure whether a write was applied.
useCases: Persistent employee repository
Persist employee edits while preventing request values from altering SQL syntax.
practices: Keep transaction ownership explicit and handle retries using stable identifiers.
database-integration.interview: Why scope a session to a unit of work? It bounds transactional state and prevents concurrent requests from sharing accidental changes.
database-integration.miniProject: Implement parameterized insert and lookup operations for employees.
exercises: Implement parameterized insert and lookup operations for employees.
Verify that an apostrophe in a name is stored literally.

validation.definition: Validation checks whether an input meets syntactic and domain requirements before acting on it.
validation.why: Prevent negative or overlapping time ranges from entering a schedule.
validation.explanation: Start with types and required fields. Check ranges and relationships between values such as start and finish. Present a precise error for a failed rule.
validation.usage: Prevent negative or overlapping time ranges from entering a schedule.

examples.title: Check a range

mistakes: Browser validation alone is bypassed by direct API clients.
edges: In Python bool is a subclass of int. Check the intended domain when accepting strict integer input.
useCases: Shift validator
Prevent negative or overlapping time ranges from entering a schedule.
practices: Apply validation at the API boundary and enforce critical constraints in the database.
validation.interview: Why combine field and cross-field validation? Some values are valid alone and invalid only in combination.
validation.miniProject: Build a validator for a start and finish hour with actionable errors.
exercises: Build a validator for a start and finish hour with actionable errors.
Test missing values, equality, the smallest hour and the largest hour.

exception-handling.definition: API exception handling translates internal failures into stable responses clients can understand.
exception-handling.why: Help a client distinguish an absent record from invalid input.
exception-handling.explanation: Identify known domain failures and give them specific statuses and public messages. Log unexpected failures with internal context and return a generic server error.
exception-handling.usage: Help a client distinguish an absent record from invalid input.
mistakes: Returning raw tracebacks can expose sensitive server details.
edges: A duplicate creation request may be a conflict even though its JSON is syntactically valid.
useCases: API error translator
Help a client distinguish an absent record from invalid input.
practices: Use consistent error codes that clients can branch on.
exception-handling.interview: Why keep a stable error code? Human-readable wording can change without breaking client behavior.
exception-handling.miniProject: Define error responses for invalid IDs, missing employees and duplicate identifiers.
exercises: Define error responses for invalid IDs, missing employees and duplicate identifiers.
Confirm unexpected failures omit private implementation details.

logging.definition: Logging records events that explain what a service did and where failures occurred.
logging.why: Trace a failed profile update without logging the employee's full request body.
logging.explanation: Give each event a consistent name and useful fields. A request identifier connects related events across several operations. Levels distinguish ordinary operation from problems requiring attention.
logging.usage: Trace a failed profile update without logging the employee's full request body.

examples.title: Select warning events
examples.code:
statuses = [200, 201, 503]
print([s for s in statuses if s >= 500])

mistakes: Logging passwords, tokens or full private payloads creates an additional copy of sensitive data.
edges: Free-form user text can include line breaks that confuse line-oriented logs.
useCases: Request activity log
Trace a failed profile update without logging the employee's full request body.
practices: Use a structured formatter and an allowlist of safe metadata.
logging.interview: How does a correlation ID help? It ties entries from one operation together without requiring private payloads.
logging.miniProject: Record named events for one successful request and one failure.
exercises: Record named events for one successful request and one failure.
Find all entries belonging to one request identifier.

api-testing.definition: A unit test checks isolated behavior. An API test sends requests through the application's HTTP boundary.
api-testing.why: Catch validation, routing and serialization bugs that direct function calls can miss.
api-testing.explanation: Arrange a known fixture, act on it and assert observable results. API tests should verify status, response schema and persisted effects using a disposable database.
api-testing.usage: Catch validation, routing and serialization bugs that direct function calls can miss.

examples.title: Assert a pure rule

mistakes: Sharing a mutable database between tests can make results depend on execution order.
edges: Returning an expected status with the wrong body still breaks a client contract.
useCases: Employee API test suite
Catch validation, routing and serialization bugs that direct function calls can miss.
practices: Test happy paths, rejected inputs and missing resources.
api-testing.interview: What does an API integration test add? It exercises the routing and request/response machinery surrounding application logic.
api-testing.miniProject: Test employee creation followed by a lookup using an isolated database.
exercises: Test employee creation followed by a lookup using an isolated database.
Check that rejected input leaves the stored row count unchanged.

backend-security.definition: Backend security limits what untrusted inputs and compromised components can do.
backend-security.why: Expose a public employee view without internal credentials or private fields.
backend-security.explanation: Map where data enters and leaves the application. Validate external input, use parameter binding, enforce resource-level authorization and return only the fields a caller needs.
backend-security.usage: Expose a public employee view without internal credentials or private fields.
mistakes: Hiding a button on the frontend cannot enforce a backend permission.
edges: A seemingly harmless response field can expose sensitive information when joined with other records.
useCases: Service boundary review
Expose a public employee view without internal credentials or private fields.
practices: Use explicit public schemas and test access with an unauthorized identity.
backend-security.interview: What is least privilege? Grant only the permissions needed for a component's current purpose.
backend-security.miniProject: Document the employee service's trust boundaries and public response fields.
exercises: Document the employee service's trust boundaries and public response fields.
Test that requesting another employee's private record is rejected.

ml-concepts.definition: Machine learning fits a rule from examples to make predictions on new inputs.
ml-concepts.why: Predict study time and compare the model with a typical past session.
ml-concepts.explanation: Features are available at prediction time. A label is the outcome to predict. A baseline provides a simple reference for deciding whether added complexity improves results.
ml-concepts.syntax:
from statistics import median
training_minutes = [10, 20, 30]
print(median(training_minutes))
ml-concepts.usage: Predict study time and compare the model with a typical past session.

examples.title: Predict with a baseline
examples.code:
from statistics import median
training_minutes = [10, 20, 30]
print(median(training_minutes))

mistakes: A feature recorded after the outcome can leak the answer during training.
edges: An accurate historical baseline may fail when future data changes.
useCases: Prediction baseline
Predict study time and compare the model with a typical past session.
practices: Define the prediction time and outcome before selecting features.
ml-concepts.interview: Why compare against a baseline? A model is useful only if its performance justifies its costs relative to a simpler rule.
ml-concepts.miniProject: Build a median-duration baseline and score it on held-out sessions.
exercises: Build a median-duration baseline and score it on held-out sessions.
Identify one candidate input unavailable at prediction time.

learning-types.definition: Supervised learning uses labeled outcomes. Unsupervised learning searches for structure without a target label.
learning-types.why: Choose between predicting an outcome and discovering recurring activity patterns.
learning-types.explanation: Predicting whether a learner returns uses known return labels. Grouping sessions by timing and length uses a similarity rule. A cluster needs interpretation before anyone assigns it a meaning.
learning-types.syntax:
records = [(10,False),(45,True)]
print([label for minutes,label in records])
learning-types.usage: Choose between predicting an outcome and discovering recurring activity patterns.

examples.title: Inspect labeled examples
examples.code:
records = [(10,False),(45,True)]
print([label for minutes,label in records])

mistakes: Interpreting a cluster identifier as a confirmed class can mislead users.
edges: Changing units can change distance-based groupings.
useCases: Session pattern explorer
Choose between predicting an outcome and discovering recurring activity patterns.
practices: State whether ground-truth labels exist and how you will evaluate the result.
learning-types.interview: What distinguishes classification from clustering? Classification predicts predefined labels while clustering proposes groups under a chosen similarity rule.
learning-types.miniProject: Compare two possible learning goals for a session dataset.
exercises: Compare two possible learning goals for a session dataset.
Explain how rescaling one feature can change cluster membership.

regression.definition: Regression predicts a numeric quantity such as minutes or cost.
regression.why: Estimate how long a lesson will take and quantify typical error in minutes.
regression.explanation: A simple linear predictor combines inputs using coefficients and an intercept. A residual is the observed value minus its prediction. Summarize error on unseen samples in units the learner understands.
regression.usage: Estimate how long a lesson will take and quantify typical error in minutes.
mistakes: Treating a predictor as a causal explanation can lead to unsupported conclusions.
edges: Extrapolating far beyond observed inputs can yield implausible predictions.
useCases: Study duration predictor
Estimate how long a lesson will take and quantify typical error in minutes.
practices: Report held-out error in the target's units.
regression.interview: What does a negative residual mean? The model predicted a value higher than the observed outcome.
regression.miniProject: Predict study duration from lesson length and report absolute errors.
exercises: Predict study duration from lesson length and report absolute errors.
Compare the line with a constant baseline on the same examples.

classification.definition: Classification assigns an example to a category using evidence from labeled cases.
classification.why: Flag sessions that may need revision while measuring unnecessary reminders.
classification.explanation: A classifier may produce a score. A threshold converts the score into a decision and trades false positives against false negatives. The appropriate threshold depends on what each error costs.
classification.syntax:
probabilities = [0.2,0.55,0.9]
print([p >= 0.6 for p in probabilities])
classification.usage: Flag sessions that may need revision while measuring unnecessary reminders.

examples.title: Apply a threshold
examples.code:
probabilities = [0.2,0.55,0.9]
print([p >= 0.6 for p in probabilities])

examples.title: Count false positives
examples.code:
truth, pred = [0,1,0], [1,1,0]
print(sum(t == 0 and p == 1 for t,p in zip(truth,pred)))

mistakes: Accuracy can look high when the important class is rare.
edges: Scores tied at a threshold require a consistent greater-than or greater-than-or-equal rule.
useCases: Revision need classifier
Flag sessions that may need revision while measuring unnecessary reminders.
practices: Choose metrics using the cost of each error type.
classification.interview: What happens if you lower the positive threshold? More examples can become positive, increasing sensitivity and potentially false alarms.
classification.miniProject: Classify revision needs at two thresholds and count errors.
exercises: Classify revision needs at two thresholds and count errors.
Explain which threshold you would use if missing a weak concept is expensive.

train-test.definition: A split reserves examples that are kept separate from training to estimate performance on new data.
train-test.why: Evaluate future learner sessions without letting their later outcomes influence training.
train-test.explanation: Use training for fitting, validation for choices and a held-out test for a final check. Split by time or entity when nearby records are related.
train-test.syntax:
days = [1,2,3,4,5]
train, test = days[:3], days[3:]
print(train, test)
train-test.usage: Evaluate future learner sessions without letting their later outcomes influence training.

examples.title: Use a temporal split
examples.code:
days = [1,2,3,4,5]
train, test = days[:3], days[3:]
print(train, test)

mistakes: Fitting preprocessing on all rows before splitting leaks information from evaluation.
edges: Repeated sessions from one learner can cross a row-level random split.
useCases: Evaluation split planner
Evaluate future learner sessions without letting their later outcomes influence training.
practices: Choose a split that mirrors the real deployment scenario.
train-test.interview: Why keep a final test apart from model selection? Repeated choices based on its results effectively fit the test set.
train-test.miniProject: Design a chronological split for predicting next week's sessions.
exercises: Design a chronological split for predicting next week's sessions.
Verify no future-derived input can enter the training partition.

feature-engineering.definition: Feature engineering converts raw observations into inputs a model can use.
feature-engineering.why: Represent a session's start hour and earlier activity without accessing its final score.
feature-engineering.explanation: Derive values from information available before predicting. Encode categories consistently and store transformations with the model so training and inference use the same representations.
feature-engineering.syntax:
known = ["Python","SQL"]
topic = "SQL"
print([int(topic == x) for x in known])
feature-engineering.usage: Represent a session's start hour and earlier activity without accessing its final score.

examples.title: Encode a category
examples.code:

topic = "SQL"
print([int(topic == x) for x in known])

mistakes: A feature using the current session's final result leaks the target.
edges: An unseen category needs a defined representation.
useCases: Session feature builder
Represent a session's start hour and earlier activity without accessing its final score.
practices: Use one fitted preprocessing pipeline for both training and inference.
feature-engineering.interview: Why avoid independent encoding at inference? A changed column order changes what the model's coefficients mean.
feature-engineering.miniProject: Build deterministic features for session start time and topic.
exercises: Build deterministic features for session start time and topic.
Define how missing history and unknown topics are represented.

model-evaluation.definition: Model evaluation measures the quality of predictions against outcomes on representative examples.
model-evaluation.why: Report duration prediction error for short and long lessons separately.
model-evaluation.explanation: Select a metric that matches the task and compare against a baseline on the same samples. Break errors down by useful groups to find behavior hidden by the overall mean.
model-evaluation.syntax:
actual, predicted = [10,30], [12,24]
print(sum(abs(a-p) for a,p in zip(actual,predicted))/len(actual))
model-evaluation.usage: Report duration prediction error for short and long lessons separately.

examples.title: Calculate MAE

mistakes: Using training performance to report expected production quality overstates generalization.
edges: Precision's denominator is zero when no positives are predicted.
useCases: Prediction scorecard
Report duration prediction error for short and long lessons separately.
practices: Include sample counts and explicit behavior for undefined metrics.
model-evaluation.interview: Why inspect subgroup errors? An overall average can conceal systematic failure for a smaller population.
model-evaluation.miniProject: Build a scorecard comparing a predictor and a baseline on identical cases.
exercises: Build a scorecard comparing a predictor and a baseline on identical cases.
Identify the three largest errors and categorize their likely causes.

overfitting.definition: Overfitting occurs when a model learns training-specific details that do not generalize.
overfitting.why: Choose model complexity using validation results and realistic constraints.
overfitting.explanation: Compare training and validation performance as capacity or training time changes. A widening gap can suggest overfitting. Also check for distribution differences and measurement problems.
overfitting.usage: Choose model complexity using validation results and realistic constraints.
mistakes: Repeated tuning on the test set turns it into a validation set.
edges: Poor training and validation results together may suggest underfitting or unsuitable features.
useCases: Learning curve review
Choose model complexity using validation results and realistic constraints.
practices: Keep one independent final test and compare simpler alternatives.
overfitting.interview: Why can lower training error be undesirable? Added capacity may fit noise and reduce performance on unseen data.
overfitting.miniProject: Plot training and validation scores for increasing model size.
exercises: Plot training and validation scores for increasing model size.
Write down evidence that would distinguish a capacity issue from data shift.

scikit-learn.definition: scikit-learn provides estimators with shared interfaces for fitting models, transforming inputs and predicting outcomes.
scikit-learn.why: Package a study-time regression model and its input transformations together.
scikit-learn.explanation: A Pipeline sequences transformations and a final estimator. Fitting it only on training data keeps fitted preprocessing consistent and reduces leakage.
scikit-learn.syntax:
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression
model = LinearRegression().fit([[1],[2],[3]],[2,4,6])
print(round(model.predict([[4]])[0]))
scikit-learn.usage: Package a study-time regression model and its input transformations together.

Package a study-time regression model and its input transformations together.

Run the framework examples in a configured development environment with the named package installed.
scikit-learn.interview: What does predict use? Parameters learned by fit and feature values for the new samples.

model-deployment.definition: Model deployment makes a fitted model available for inference under a defined contract.
model-deployment.why: Serve a duration estimate with enough metadata to trace which model produced it.
model-deployment.explanation: Version the model with its preprocessing, expected schema and training metadata. Validate incoming requests, monitor failures and retain a previously tested version for recovery.
model-deployment.usage: Serve a duration estimate with enough metadata to trace which model produced it.

edges: A schema-compatible numeric field can silently change units.
useCases: Versioned prediction endpoint
Serve a duration estimate with enough metadata to trace which model produced it.
practices: Test a known inference example through the deployed entry point.
model-deployment.interview: Why deploy preprocessing with the model? The model expects the exact representation used for training.
model-deployment.miniProject: Specify a prediction endpoint with version metadata and input validation.
exercises: Specify a prediction endpoint with version metadata and input validation.
Rehearse switching back to a previous tested model.

llms.definition: A large language model estimates a distribution over possible next tokens given a context.
llms.why: Design an assistant that checks unsupported factual answers against source material.
llms.explanation: Generation repeatedly chooses a token and extends the context. Training captures statistical regularities, so fluent output can still contain false claims. An application's evidence and checks determine whether an answer is usable.
llms.usage: Design an assistant that checks unsupported factual answers against source material.

Design an assistant that checks unsupported factual answers against source material.

llms.miniProject: Sketch a toy next-token distribution and trace one generation step.
exercises: Sketch a toy next-token distribution and trace one generation step.
Identify which facts in a sample answer require supporting evidence.

tokens.definition: A tokenizer divides content into units a model processes. A context window bounds the token sequence available to a request.
tokens.why: Decide how many passages fit in a document question-answering request.
tokens.explanation: Token counts depend on the model's tokenizer, language and formatting. Budget instructions, history, retrieved material and a reserve for the response. Count using the configured provider's tokenizer when exact limits matter.
tokens.usage: Decide how many passages fit in a document question-answering request.

Decide how many passages fit in a document question-answering request.

tokens.interview: Why can identical character lengths yield different token counts? Tokenization depends on sequences and the tokenizer vocabulary.
tokens.miniProject: Calculate a passage budget from a model limit and measured component lengths.

prompt-engineering.definition: Prompt engineering specifies a task, context and desired response so a model can attempt it consistently.
prompt-engineering.why: Ask an assistant to answer a document question and cite a passage identifier.
prompt-engineering.explanation: Make the input and expected output explicit. Provide representative examples for ambiguous cases. Evaluate changes on fixed inputs, including cases with insufficient evidence.
prompt-engineering.syntax:
question = "When does the lab open?"
prompt = f"Answer using the passage. If insufficient, say unknown.\nQuestion: {question}"
print(prompt.splitlines()[-1])
prompt-engineering.usage: Ask an assistant to answer a document question and cite a passage identifier.

prompt-engineering.interview: How would you evaluate a prompt edit? Compare old and new behavior on the same representative cases with predefined criteria.
prompt-engineering.miniProject: Write a grounded-answer prompt including a rule for missing evidence.

model-apis.definition: A model API accepts a structured request and returns generated output or an error through a network service.
model-apis.why: Connect an optional feedback provider without blocking local lessons.
model-apis.explanation: Keep provider configuration and credentials on the server. Set a timeout and a bounded retry policy. Preserve the difference between an unavailable provider and a successful generated result.
model-apis.usage: Connect an optional feedback provider without blocking local lessons.
mistakes: Retrying all failures including invalid credentials wastes time and money.
edges: A timeout after remote processing can leave the caller uncertain whether usage was billed.
useCases: Provider request adapter
Connect an optional feedback provider without blocking local lessons.
practices: Limit retry attempts, honor provider retry guidance and avoid logging private prompts by default.
model-apis.interview: Why isolate a provider adapter? The rest of the app can use a stable interface while provider details and errors vary.
model-apis.miniProject: Design an adapter with explicit success, unavailable and invalid-request outcomes.
exercises: Design an adapter with explicit success, unavailable and invalid-request outcomes.
Test its fallback behavior with a deliberately absent API key.

structured-outputs.definition: Structured output constrains a generated response to a machine-readable shape.
structured-outputs.why: Accept feedback only if its score is in range and the cited concept exists.
structured-outputs.explanation: Parse the response, validate fields and types, then apply domain-specific checks. A schema-valid response can still contain unsupported claims or invalid references.
structured-outputs.syntax:
data = {"score":82}
print(type(data["score"]) is int and 0 <= data["score"] <= 100)
structured-outputs.usage: Accept feedback only if its score is in range and the cited concept exists.

Accept feedback only if its score is in range and the cited concept exists.
practices: Report parse, schema and semantic failures separately.
structured-outputs.interview: Can a schema prove a factual explanation is true? It constrains representation and requires separate evidence checks.
structured-outputs.miniProject: Validate a feedback object with a score, known concepts and an explanation.
exercises: Validate a feedback object with a score, known concepts and an explanation.

embeddings.definition: An embedding maps an input to a numerical vector in a learned representation space.
embeddings.why: Find document passages whose representations are near a question's representation.
embeddings.explanation: Compare vectors produced by compatible models and preprocessing. Cosine similarity measures the angle between nonzero vectors, emphasizing orientation rather than magnitude.
embeddings.syntax:
a, b = [1,2], [3,4]
print(sum(x*y for x,y in zip(a,b)))
embeddings.usage: Find document passages whose representations are near a question's representation.

embeddings.miniProject: Rank three toy passage vectors against one query using cosine similarity.

vector-databases.definition: A vector database stores embeddings with identifiers and metadata and retrieves near neighbors for a query.
vector-databases.why: Restrict retrieval to passages the learner may access.
vector-databases.explanation: Index construction trades memory, query time and recall. Metadata filters restrict eligible records. An update must keep document identity, text, version and vector aligned.
